extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent practitioners/applicants
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for patent examiners (and applicants) on evaluating whether claim language meets the threshold requirements of clarity and precision under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (pre‑AIA 112 second paragraph), including how to record, communicate, and resolve indefiniteness issues during prosecution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply broadest reasonable interpretation during examination
rubrics_metrics.description: During examination apply the broadest reasonable interpretation (BRI) to the claim because the patent record is in development and not fixed during examination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: BRI is applied to facilitate sharpening and clarifying claims at the application stage. The lower threshold is applied because the agency does not rely on the prosecution record for claim interpretation. See cited cases (e.g., In re Zletz; In re Buszard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness standard — metes and bounds must be clear
rubrics_metrics.description: After applying BRI, if the metes and bounds of the claimed invention are not clear, the claim is indefinite and should be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 112(b) (or pre‑AIA 112, second paragraph).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a POSITA would read the claim with more than one reasonable interpretation, rejection under 112(b) is appropriate. Examiners are cautioned against conflating mere claim breadth with indefiniteness; a claim can be broad yet definite if its boundaries are clear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Threshold requirements of clarity and precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The examiner’s focus is whether the claim meets the threshold statutory requirements of clarity ('particularity' and 'distinctness'), not whether better language exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims must set out and circumscribe a particular subject matter with a reasonable degree of clarity and particularity so they notify the public of what is and is not protected. Some latitude in expression is permitted so long as 35 U.S.C. 112(b) is satisfied.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three‑factor definiteness analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Definiteness of claim language must be analyzed in light of: (A) the content of the particular application disclosure; (B) the teachings of the prior art; and (C) the claim interpretation a person of ordinary skill in the art would give at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners must consider these factors together when determining whether the claim apprises a POSITA of its scope and thus serves the notice function required by 112(b).

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the claim as a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing for compliance with 112(b), the examiner must consider the claim as a whole to determine whether it apprises one of ordinary skill in the art of its scope and serves the notice function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Totality of limitations and their interaction with each other must be considered (e.g., In re Larsen). A claim that does not allow a POSITA to determine how to avoid infringement may be rejected.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not use per se rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Office policy is not to employ per se rules to make technical rejections for indefiniteness; examples are fact specific and should not be applied as per se rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should rely on case‑specific analysis rather than automatic rejections based on particular language forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner must establish a clear record
rubrics_metrics.description: When asserting a prima facie indefiniteness rejection, the examiner should provide a complete and accurate picture of the Office’s consideration and clearly explain the basis for the rejection in the file history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide clear explanations of actions taken during prosecution and avoid mere conclusions that a term is indefinite; see MPEP §§ 1302.14, 707.07(f), 706.03, 707.07(g).

rubrics_metrics.name: Office action must provide a sufficient explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: An Office action asserting indefiniteness must set forth the specific term or phrase that is indefinite and why the metes and bounds are unclear so the applicant can prepare a meaningful response.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because the rejection obliges the applicant to explain or amend, the Office action should include enough detail (and where practicable, indicate ways to resolve the indefiniteness) to permit a meaningful reply. Cite Halliburton and related case law on public notice function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make a prima facie case for indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: To make a prima facie case of indefiniteness the examiner should point out the specific term/phrase, explain in detail why it renders the metes and bounds unclear, and, whenever practicable, indicate how deficiencies may be corrected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the applicant fails to adequately respond to that prima facie case, the examiner may make the indefiniteness rejection final (see MPEP § 707.07(d) and Packard).

rubrics_metrics.name: Suggest claim language but do not impose preferences
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiners are encouraged to suggest claim language to improve clarity or precision, but should not insist on their own preferences if applicant’s language meets statutory requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The focus is on whether language satisfies 112(b), not on stylistic preferences. If more information is necessary to ascertain meaning, a requirement under 37 CFR 1.105 may be appropriate (see MPEP § 704.10).

rubrics_metrics.name: Resolve ambiguity during prosecution where possible
rubrics_metrics.description: It is highly desirable to have applicants resolve claim ambiguities by amending claims during prosecution rather than leaving resolution to later litigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicant may amend claims or provide persuasive explanations (including art‑recognized dictionary definitions or declarations) to show how a POSITA would understand claim language. If examiner finds applicant persuasive, note withdrawal of prior rejection and explain why position changed to improve prosecution record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain reasons for allowance when record unclear
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 CFR 1.104(e), if the prosecution record does not make clear why a claim is allowable, the examiner may set forth the claim interpretation and reasons for allowance in the reasons for allowance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This improves the quality and reliability of issued patents and aids public evaluation; however, avoid placing unwarranted broad or narrow interpretations on the claims in those statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attempt interview when indefiniteness is sole issue
rubrics_metrics.description: When indefiniteness is the only issue, attempt to resolve the matter through an examiner interview before resorting to a rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interviews can clarify BRI, meanings of limitations, preamble scope, functional language, means‑plus‑function limitations, etc. The substance of any interview must be made of record in the application (MPEP § 713.04; 37 CFR 1.2).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must correspond to claims (antecedent basis/support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim terms must find clear support or antecedent basis in the specification so their meaning may be ascertained by reference to the specification (37 CFR 1.75(d)(1)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Glossaries are helpful. If the specification lacks needed support, object to the specification under 37 CFR 1.75(d)(1) and require amendment (see MPEP §§ 608.01(o), 2181, IV). Applicant must amend description or claims without introducing new matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims inconsistent with specification may be indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim clear on its face may still be indefinite if a conflict or inconsistency between the claimed subject matter and the specification disclosure renders the scope uncertain.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Internal inconsistencies between claim terms and descriptions/definitions in the specification can cause indefiniteness (examples: In re Moore; In re Cohn; In re Anderson).

rubrics_metrics.name: Breadth is not indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: A broad claim is not indefinite merely because it covers a wide scope of subject matter provided the scope is clearly defined; indefiniteness occurs when boundaries are not clearly delineated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If undue breadth arises from other issues, other statutes may apply: lack of support/enabling → 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (first paragraph); reading on prior art → 35 U.S.C. 102/103; claims broader than disclosed by extrinsic statements → 112(b) may be appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meaning of every term should be apparent
rubrics_metrics.description: The meaning of every term used in a claim should be apparent from the prior art or from the specification and drawings at the time the application was filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claim language may not be ambiguous, vague, incoherent, opaque, or otherwise unclear in describing/defining the claimed invention. New terms are allowed but must be made clear by the specification; see In re Morris, In re Prater, In re Zletz and related MPEP cross‑references.

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance required precision with limitations of language/technology
rubrics_metrics.description: The requirement for clarity and precision must be balanced with the limitations of language and science; claims must be as precise as the subject matter permits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If claims, read in light of the specification, reasonably apprise skilled artisans of utilization and scope, and language is as precise as subject permits, statutory demands are met. If not, examiner should provide reasons and suggest alternatives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms used contrary to ordinary meaning must be redefined
rubrics_metrics.description: If applicant uses terms contrary to their ordinary meaning, the written description must clearly redefine the terms so that POSITA is put on notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentee may be his own lexicographer, but the written description must clearly redefine the term (see Process Control Corp. v. HydReclaim Corp.; Hormone Research Foundation v. Genentech). Compare to technical dictionaries as appropriate (MPEP § 2111.01).

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative terminology and terms of degree require standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Relative terminology (terms of degree) does not automatically render a claim indefinite; acceptability depends on whether a POSITA would understand what is claimed in light of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If spec provides a standard for measuring degree (examples, figures, recognized standards), terms of degree may be definite. If not, determine whether POSITA can nonetheless ascertain scope or whether applicant can supply evidence (eg, 37 CFR 1.132 declaration) to overcome rejection (cases: Interval Licensing, Enzo Biochem, Seattle Box).

rubrics_metrics.name: Reference to a variable object may render claim indefinite
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim may be indefinite if it refers to an object that is variable (e.g., 'height of the rider') without specifying standards for the variable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples (Miyazaki; Brummer) show that without a known standard relating the variable to the claimed structure, indefiniteness can result. Conversely, relational sizing based on objective features (e.g., insertable through car doorframe) can be definite if reasonably precise for the subject matter (Orthokinetics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations — interpret 'about' in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Ranges expressed by terms like 'about' must be determined in context of the specification and claims; whether 'about' is definite depends on whether the context allows one to determine the encompassed range.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law (e.g., Ortho‑McNeil, W.L. Gore, Amgen) instructs that 'about' can be definite when objective measurement is available, but may be indefinite when close prior art exists and no contextual guidance exists in spec or prosecution history.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approximations — 'essentially' may be definite with guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases like 'essentially free of' can be definite if the specification contains guidelines and examples that enable a POSITA to draw a line between unavoidable impurities and essential ingredients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: In re Marosi held 'essentially free of alkali metal' definite because the specification provided examples and guidelines; patent law does not require specification of an exact numeric cutoff when impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common specific topics to check for indefiniteness
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequently recurring indefiniteness issues include functional claim limitations, relative terminology/terms of degree, lack of antecedent basis, new terminology, means‑plus‑function concerns, and references to variable objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: MPEP § 2173.05 provides detailed examples and rationales (fact‑specific) for these topics; use those examples for guidance but analyze each claim in its factual context.
